description: I'm Mohamed Hamdy, an AI/ML Engineer passionate about solving real-world problems using Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Computer Vision. I'm interested in geospatial AI, satellite data, and environmental challenges. I can contribute to Python development, data processing, and model building. I'm looking for motivated teammates with skills in GIS, remote sensing, satellite imagery, data analysis, and software development.
summary:
Delta Sentry is an early-warning system for crop health in Egypt's Nile Delta. Egypt farms a thin strip of irrigated land, and district averages hide field-level failure: by the time a problem is visible from the road, it is already a loss.

We built a working web application that fuses 30-metre NASA HLS imagery with a fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0 foundation model to forecast next month's vegetation, compares that forecast against what the satellite actually observed, and converts the disagreement into a ranked list of contiguous field patches. An inspector opens the site, sees 59 flagged blocks and the 12 worth visiting first, and prints a field order with coordinates and an observation checklist.

We audited 44 flagged patches against high-resolution imagery and published the result: 18 confirmed decline, 26 classified as harvest, cloud artefact or unclear. We report our error budget openly, including the baselines we do not beat.
details:
Delta Sentry turns a satellite forecast error into a work order.

THE PROBLEM

Egypt grows its food on a thin strip of irrigated land along the Nile. When a block of fields begins to fail, district-level averages do not move: a governorate mean stays flat while a hundred hectares go under, and by the time the loss is visible from the road it is already a compensation claim. Satellite monitoring of Egyptian agriculture is not new. What is missing is the step between a map and a decision. An agronomist cannot act on a raster of NDVI values, but they can act on a short list with a place, an area and a reason.

HOW IT WORKS

The pipeline runs in five steps.

1. We extract 30 m Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel imagery and 25 years of MODIS NDVI through NASA AppEEARS.

2. Every scene is cloud-masked with Fmask and reduced to monthly median composites.

3. A fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M model, with a frozen backbone and a custom U-Net decoder, predicts next month's NDVI from the previous four months of imagery.

4. The forecast is subtracted from what the satellite actually observed. Negative gaps are clustered into contiguous field patches.

5. Patches are ranked by area and exported as a printable field order with coordinates and an observation checklist.

An inspector opens one page and sees 59 flagged patches covering 175 feddan, and the 12 worth driving to first.

EVIDENCE, INCLUDING WHAT FAILS

We trained on 500 spatial-temporal samples spanning 2013 to 2023 and evaluated on held-out 2025 data. Seasonal climatology scores an RMSE of 0.1767, persistence 0.1858, and our model 0.1823. We beat persistence by 1.9 percent and we do not beat climatology. A 12-year same-month climatology is a genuinely strong baseline for a seasonal signal, and we say so on the site rather than in a footnote.

What we claim is narrower and testable: the model produces a spatial ranking that a climatology cannot, because a climatology is smooth across space by construction. A district average and a climatology are both blind to which field is failing. That is the gap this project fills.

We also audited 44 flagged patches one by one against high-resolution imagery. Eighteen, or 40.9 percent, showed a visible vegetation decline. Twelve were normal harvest or crop rotation, nine were cloud or sensor artefact, and five were unclear. We publish the 26 failures because a false-alarm rate is the number a ministry needs before it trusts a list.

Separately, a pixel-wise Seasonal Mann-Kendall test with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction on 25 years of MODIS found 78.6 percent of the area significantly greening, 21.4 percent with no significant trend, and 0.04 percent declining. The Delta is greening in aggregate, which is exactly why district averages hide the blocks that matter.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The direct benefit is time. An inspector with a vehicle and a finite week gets a ranked shortlist instead of a district to drive around. The second benefit is early warning: the alert fires when reality departs from a model's expectation, which can happen before the decline is visible to the eye. The intended impact is a working interface between satellite data and a field visit, at a cost a governorate can carry, because the whole application is a static site and the model runs on a free hosting tier.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python, PyTorch, TerraTorch, Xarray, Rasterio, NumPy and pymannkendall for the science. FastAPI on a Hugging Face Docker Space for live inference. A zero-dependency HTML, CSS and JavaScript front end with canvas rendering, no framework and no build step, so the entire application runs from a static host and loads without a server.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The first creative decision was to build the product around the forecast error rather than the forecast. Most vegetation models are judged on how close they get to reality. We treat the distance from reality as the signal: a model that is confidently wrong is not a failure here, it is an alert. The second decision was to end the pipeline at a printable field order rather than a map, because the unit of action for an inspector is a visit, not a pixel. The third was to make the model runnable from the browser, so a judge or a ministry officer can press one button and watch inference happen rather than take our word for it.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Cloud cover over the Delta, which is why every scene is masked before compositing. The difference between seasonal senescence and genuine stress, which is why a flagged block is labelled bare soil when that is what the data shows instead of being called a stressed crop. The cost of a false alarm to a ministry with limited vehicles, which is why we audited our own alerts and published the failures. And the risk of presenting a prototype as a finished service, which is why every claim in the application is paired with its limit.

LIMITS

This is one pilot tile of about 12 square kilometres in Kafr El-Sheikh, not the Delta. An alert is an indicator for investigation, not a diagnosis of crop failure. Patch coordinates are mapped from the grid and are approximate, not surveyed GPS. In the December pilot month the district-wide NDVI drop is partly harvest and bare soil rather than stress. Re-basing the anomaly on same-month multi-year climatology, masking cells below NDVI 0.05, and adding Sentinel-1 SAR to separate harvest from failure are the next steps.
